newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S., Japan to discuss insurance in Washington.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan to discuss insurance in Washington.

text.p: Japan's Finance Minister Wataru Kubo and U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky will meet to discuss bilateral insurance trade in Washington around the time of the meeting of G7 countries that starts at the end of this month, U.S. Ambassador to Japan Walter Mondale said on Wednesday.
"It's an important meeting which will be taken seriously by both sides," Mondale said after a meeting with Kubo.
Although Mondale did not disclose details of his talks with Kubo, he called it a "good meeting".

The finance ministers and central bankers of the Group of Seven industrialised countries are due to meet in Washington on September 28 at the time of the annual meetings of the IMF/World Bank, which are to run until October 3.
A Japanese Finance Ministry official told reporters that the exact time of the Kubo-Barshefsky meeting had yet to be set.
He said Kubo and Mondale had agreed that the talks over the insurance dispute were proceeding, but that gaps remained. They also agreed to work towards taking the discussions further, he said.
Asked if the two talked about setting conditions on the operations of Japanese insurance subsidiaries, the official said the two discussed the issue but he declined to give details.

Asked whether Mondale talked about the United States implementing sanctions against Japan if Tokyo did not uphold a 1994 bilateral pact on deregulating its insurance market, the official said no such mention was made.

The official added that it could be difficult for Kubo and Barshefsky to have substantive talks in Washington as Kubo's schedule was tight. At the moment there were no working level talks scheduled in Washington, he said.
Although it would not be good to prolong the settlement of the dispute more than necessary the two sides had not so far set any definite deadline for reaching an agreement, he said.

On Tuesday, U.S. President Bill Clinton, in a meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in New York, urged mutual efforts to resolve a dispute over implementation the 1994 pact, as well as a dispute over aviation.

Negotiators from the Finance Ministry and the U.S. Trade Representative's office have already failed to meet a July 31 deadline for resolving the insurance dispute, and working-level talks last week left the two sides far apart.

The insurance dispute centres on U.S. allegations that Tokyo is poised to renege on the 1994 pact by opening up its so-called "third-sector" niche market -- which is profitable for foreign firms -- before substantially deregulating primary life and non-life insurance business, where domestic firms hold sway.
